solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Always backing Adam's mate (Labour right-winger)

indicators.note: the right wing of a written word is its far end, so only its final letter is kept

blocks.note: backing a cause means being in favour of it
Eve was Adam's partner in Genesis
the word's final letter

explanation.surface: A political loyalist who has always supported the partner of a Labour Party right-winger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like a reversal signal but simply means supporting. 'Right-winger' sounds like a political label; here it is the rightmost letter of Labour.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean at all times, without end; the adverb can replace the other in any sentence.

clue.text: China kicks out King and his sort – diabolical!

indicators.note: kicking someone out removes them, so a letter is thrown out of the word
to sort things is to rearrange them into a different order

blocks.note: rhyming slang: china plate = mate, so a friend
R stands for Rex, Latin for king
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An outraged complaint that China expels a king and his kind, called diabolical.
explanation.walkthrough: China is Cockney rhyming slang (china plate = mate), a staple of British slang. 'His sort' reads as 'his type of person' but is an instruction to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fiendish is wicked like a devil, a direct synonym for diabolical in everyday use.

clue.text: Dicky tries to engage once more in parliamentary business?

definitions.text: to engage once more in parliamentary business?
definitions.note: cryptic: Parliament 'sits', so to engage again is to re-sit

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for faulty or unsound, so the letters are in a broken order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A shaky attempt by someone to get back into Parliament's work.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a playful definition: Parliament is said to sit when in session, so a second sitting is a re-sit, normally an exam taken again.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliament is described as sitting during sessions, so sitting again punningly means returning to the business of the house.

clue.text: Beer name on can clutched by very old screen idol

indicators.note: something clutched is held tightly in a grip, so outer letters surround the rest

blocks.note: V is the standard abbreviation for very
ale is a type of beer
N is the abbreviation for name
a tin is a can
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A beer can bearing the name of a famous old film star.
explanation.walkthrough: Rudolph Valentino was the great romantic star of 1920s silent films.
explanation.definitionFit: Valentino was a celebrated heart-throb of silent cinema, an example of a film star idolised by audiences.

clue.text: Public performance of filthy article

indicators.note: something filthy is messed up and spoiled, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A show staging a smutty piece of writing in public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filthy article' reads like a dirty magazine piece, very Private Eye, but 'article' is just the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A recital is a concert or reading given by a performer before an audience, so an example of a public show.

clue.text: Endless resentment associated with pole dancing cover

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off
dancing moves things around, so the letters change places

blocks.note: envy is resentment of what another has
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Jealousy linked to pole dancing, with something hiding it from view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole dancing' reads as the strip-club activity; 'dancing' is only telling you to rearrange the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To envelop is to wrap or surround completely, so it is a verb synonym for cover.

clue.text: Bust near leg? Pad out

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so the letters are broken up and reset

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Breasts or thighs, and padding to make them look bigger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' wants to be a noun near a leg, part of the body; it is a verb meaning broken.
explanation.definitionFit: Padding something out makes it bigger or fuller, which is exactly the sense of the verb to make larger.

clue.text: On the way out, not dead but very striving

indicators.note: 'not' says this letter is absent, so it is taken away

blocks.note: V is the abbreviation for very
someone dying is on their way out of life
D is the abbreviation for dead

explanation.surface: Someone close to death but still fighting hard.
explanation.walkthrough: The dead letter is dropped from the front of DYING and V for very takes its place.
explanation.definitionFit: Vying means competing hard against rivals, so it is a synonym for striving in the sense of contending.

clue.text: John, pre-eminent male, performing – or being a spectator

blocks.note: john is slang for a toilet
a king is the top man
a performer is on stage

explanation.surface: A man called John, top dog, either performing himself or just watching.
explanation.walkthrough: John looks like a man's name but is the toilet (US slang, also used in Britain), the LOO.
explanation.definitionFit: To look on is to watch something happen without taking part, which is what spectators do.

clue.text: One who pulls plug on Brenda?

blocks.note: to plug a product is to puff it, promote it
Private Eye calls the late Queen Brenda; ER is Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Someone who switches off Brenda's life support.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II, hence ER. 'Pulls plug' suggests ending life support, but 'pulls' belongs with 'One who' as a smoker drawing on a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoker pulls on a cigarette or pipe, drawing smoke in with short breaths, which is puffing.

clue.text: Support when wife leaves sly, furtive type

indicators.note: when someone leaves they go away, so that letter departs from the word

blocks.note: a weasel is a sneaky, untrustworthy person
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: Backing a sneaky character once his wife walks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' sounds like emotional support for a deserted husband; it is the stand a painter rests a canvas on.
explanation.definitionFit: An easel is a wooden frame that holds up a painting or board, so a kind of physical stand.

clue.text: Phone sex dodgy? Cancel!

blocks.note: to phone someone is to call them
'it' is a coy word for sex
food that is dodgy has gone off

explanation.surface: A worried caller deciding a phone-sex line is too risky and ending it.
explanation.walkthrough: Each word is read on its own: the phone gives the call, 'it' is old slang for sex, and dodgy means off.
explanation.definitionFit: To call something off is an idiom for abandoning a planned event, so a phrasal equivalent of cancel.

clue.text: One who initiates a bang – aroused, ardent too!

indicators.note: aroused means stirred up, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A lover who starts a sexual encounter, excited and passionate as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bang' is slang for sex and 'aroused, ardent' keeps the bedroom picture going, but the bang is an explosion.
explanation.definitionFit: A detonator is the device that sets off an explosive charge, so it literally starts an explosion.

clue.text: Hold on to amphetamine, bitch!

blocks.note: to grip something is to keep a firm hold of it
E is ecstasy, an amphetamine-type drug

explanation.surface: Someone told to keep hold of the speed, addressed as a bitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitch' looks like an insult at the end of an order; it is the verb meaning to complain.
explanation.definitionFit: To bitch and to gripe are both slang verbs for complaining in a moaning, grumbling way.

clue.text: (&17/26) Putin's war – "anti-imperialist core ploy" – goes pear-shaped when America intervenes

indicators.note: to intervene is to come in between, so a letter is placed among the others
going pear-shaped means going wrong, so the letters fall out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
A is the abbreviation for America

explanation.surface: Russia's invasion, sold as an anti-imperialist plan, falls apart once the United States steps in.
explanation.walkthrough: The A for America is added to the quoted phrase before the whole lot is rearranged. Putin's government insisted the 2022 invasion of Ukraine be called by this euphemism.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kremlin's official euphemism for its invasion of Ukraine avoided calling it a war, so the phrase names that conflict.

clue.text: Exuberant wild teen hold balls against one

indicators.note: something wild is unruly and out of order, so the letters are rearranged
to hold something is to keep it within, so the outer letters wrap around
against means up next to, so the two pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
balls and bull both mean nonsense
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A lively, unruly teenager clutching balls against somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' looks like sports equipment or anatomy, but here it is British slang for nonsense, which is also what 'bull' means.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebullient describes someone bubbling over with cheerful energy, a close synonym of exuberant.

clue.text: A burning hate for this guy?

definitions.text: A burning hate for this guy?

blocks.note: surface: someone loathes a particular man with a fierce passion
setter: a guy is the dummy burnt on Bonfire Night; a hated figure is burnt in model form

explanation.walkthrough: On Bonfire Night (5 November) British people burn a stuffed figure of Guy Fawkes called a guy; protesters likewise burn models of hated leaders.
explanation.definitionFit: A crude model of a person, burned or hanged in protest, shows hatred toward the figure it represents.

clue.text: A selfish Tory leader crushed – untrustworthy

indicators.note: a leader comes at the front, so the opening letter is taken
something crushed is mangled out of shape, so the letters are reformed

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter

explanation.surface: A self-serving Conservative leader defeated and branded disloyal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tory leader' sounds like a party head being crushed at the polls; it supplies only one letter to join the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Faithless means disloyal or not to be relied upon, a synonym for untrustworthy.

clue.text: see 13ac.
Brown accepts Hello bribe

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: buff is a yellowish-brown colour
yo is a slang greeting

explanation.surface: A politician named Brown takes a backhander from Hello! magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown reads as Gordon Brown and Hello as the celebrity magazine; they are a colour and a greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: To buy someone off is to pay them to stay quiet or cooperate, an idiom meaning to bribe.

clue.text: Cold inside, is fast moving far to the right

indicators.note: moving shifts things about, so the letters change position
inside means placed within, so one piece sits in the middle of the other

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Indoors it is chilly, and politics is lurching quickly rightwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast moving' reads as a speedy drift, but 'moving' is the instruction to rearrange 'is fast'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fascism sits at the authoritarian extreme of the right wing, so the adjective describes extreme right-wing politics.

clue.text: Conservative starts to have invitations accepted – Number Ten includes drink!

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative

blocks.clueFragment: have invitations accepted – Number Ten includes
blocks.note: the opening letter of each of these six words

explanation.surface: Tories receive invitations, and Downing Street's parties include alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: Number Ten is 10 Downing Street, the Prime Minister's residence, recalling the lockdown parties. The run of first letters stretches across the dash.
explanation.definitionFit: Chianti is a red wine from Tuscany, so it is one example of an alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: 'Gotcha!' in editorial, somewhat restrained

indicators.note: somewhat means only partly, so just a portion of the word is used

blocks.note: the closing part of the exclamation
taken as written
ED is the abbreviation for editor or editorial

explanation.surface: A newspaper leader crowing 'Gotcha!' at an opponent, though fairly muted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gotcha!' recalls The Sun's notorious Falklands headline. 'Somewhat' looks like it qualifies 'restrained' but trims the exclamation to its last three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Being chained is being held back by physical fetters, so it is a strong synonym for restrained.

clue.text: Having an erection, Henry (advanced in years) gets support

blocks.note: having an erection is being up
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
someone advanced in years is old

explanation.surface: An elderly man named Henry, aroused, receives some help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets support' sounds like Henry needing Viagra or a walking stick; 'gets' only joins, and support is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To uphold a decision or principle is to back it and keep it standing, a verb synonym for support.

clue.text: Fortune can be a pain in the arse

blocks.note: first meaning: heaps of cash, great wealth
second meaning: haemorrhoids, a literal anal ailment

explanation.surface: Wealth turning out to be more trouble than it is worth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A pain in the arse' is British slang for a nuisance, but here it is meant literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Piles can mean a large fortune, as in making piles, and is also the everyday name for haemorrhoids.

clue.text: Soak pissed over hospital cap

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunk letters stagger out of order
in a down entry, letters going over another piece spread across it, so one sits within

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A drunk collapsing outside a hospital, with a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: A soak is a heavy drinker, which makes 'pissed' fit the picture; both words are wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A shako is a tall cylindrical military hat with a peak and plume, an example of headgear.

clue.text: A lot of money invested in processed shit pet food

indicators.note: to invest is to put something into a venture, so one piece is placed inside another
processing changes raw material into a new form, so the letters are remade

blocks.note: taken as written
G is a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A fortune spent on rubbish processed pet food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet food' looks like the definition, but 'pet' belongs to the letters being rearranged and only 'food' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaghetti is long thin pasta, so one example of something people eat.

clue.text: Common vegetable – extremely tiresome when stuck into sailor

indicators.note: extremes are the two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept
something stuck into another is pushed inside it

blocks.note: a tar is a sailor
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A dull everyday vegetable stuck to a sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: TAR, Jack tar, is the old nickname for a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: Tater is informal, chiefly British and dialect, for potato, the most ordinary vegetable there is.

clue.text: see 13ac.
Spear-carrier in unisex trainers?

indicators.note: 'in' says the letters sit within the following words, spanning their boundary

blocks.note: the letters run across the join between the two words

explanation.surface: A soldier carrying a spear while wearing gender-neutral sports shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spear-carrier' is theatre slang for a walk-on part, the soldier who stands at the back with a spear.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-speaking background performer in a play or film is a minor role filler, the classic spear-carrier.

clue.text: City responsible for Heath retiring? "Having one in balls"

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing, going back the way one came
'in' places one piece inside another

blocks.note: Ted Heath was the Conservative prime minister of 1970 to 1974
balls and rot both mean nonsense
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A city that caused Edward Heath to step down, with a crude quote attached.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Heath, British prime minister in the 1970s, was known as Ted. Balls is British slang for nonsense, as is rot.
explanation.definitionFit: Detroit is the Michigan motor city, an example of a large American urban centre.

clue.text: Ed's ballsed up against Tory rabble – waste

indicators.note: ballsed up is British slang for botched, so these letters are messed up
a rabble is a disorderly crowd, so these letters are in disarray

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Ed Miliband botches it against a mob of Conservatives, a wasted effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waste' reads as a noun summing up the fiasco, but it is the verb, as in to lay waste.
explanation.definitionFit: To waste a place or enemy is slang for wrecking or killing, the same sense as destroy.
